Comment: noROI(input). Codes object and contextual information and serves as a major input source to hippocampus (DG/CA3). Projects via perforant path.
noROI(input). Codes spatial information and grid cell activity and serves as a major input source to hippocampus (DG/CA3). Projects via perforant path.
Output Semantics: [MEC-L2] Spatial location and movement information. Grid cell-based hexagonal spatial representation;

Comment: noROI(input). Codes spatial information and temporal control signals. Projects directly to CA1 (temporoammonic pathway).
Output Semantics: [MEC-L3] Spatial information and temporal control signals. Supervisory signal that modulates CA1 temporal coding;

Comment: noROI(input). Codes contextual information. Projects directly to CA1 (temporoammonic pathway).
Output Semantics: [LEC-L3] Contextual information. Episodic context and environmental states;

Comment: Within ROI. Granule cells of dentate gyrus. Implements pattern separation of input patterns and transforms similar stimuli into distinguishable representations. Projects to CA3 via mossy fibers.
Requirement realization by interface: [DG] Pattern-separated stimulus representation. Sparse and orthogonalized input patterns;
Capability: For associative memory formation, input stimuli must be transformed into distinguishable representations to prevent interference between similar stimuli. Input: object/context information from [U.LEC-L2] ([LEC-L2] object feature representation) and spatial information from [U.MEC-L2] ([MEC-L2] spatial location and movement information). Output: sparse and orthogonalized stimulus representation from [U.DG] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation). DG transforms similar input patterns into output patterns with minimal overlap.
Mechanism: Interface receives object/context/spatial information from [U.LEC-L2] and [U.MEC-L2] as input, and sends pattern-separated representations to [U.CA3-Pyr] and [U.CA3-IN] as output. This matches the function defined in Requirement: transformation of similar stimuli into distinguishable representations.
Implementation: Pattern separation: Computational transformation of high-dimensional similar inputs into low-overlap outputs. This function is based on the computational theory of dentate gyrus proposed by O'Reilly & McClelland (1994). Pattern separation is closely related to competitive learning and sparse coding. Experiments by Rolls (2013) and Leutgeb et al. (2007) confirmed that DG generates representations with minimal overlap. In computational neuroscience, it is defined as transformation to sparse distributed representations (Marr, 1971).
column12: DG achieves sparse firing through input integration in granule cell dendrites and threshold control. Specifically, (1) high firing threshold, (2) strong feedforward inhibition, (3) nonlinear integration in dendrites, and (4) feedback inhibition from mossy cells result in only a few percent of granule cells being active overall (Myers & Scharfman, 2011). This low activity rate reduces overlap between similar inputs. Furthermore, heterogeneity of adult-born neurons and semilunar granule cells (SGCs) contributes to dynamic sparsity control (2024 research).
column13: [U.DG] = sparse([U.LEC-L2], [U.MEC-L2]), where sparse(x) represents a high-dimensional, low-overlap transformation with activity level ~2-5% of total granule cells

Comment: Within ROI. CA3 pyramidal cells. Form the core of associative memory and form associations between different stimuli through recurrent connections (heteroassociative memory). Recall complete memories from partial cues via pattern completion. Project to CA1 via Schaffer collaterals.
column14: [CA3-Pyr] Representation of associated stimulus pairs. Associations between stimuli formed by recurrent circuits and pattern completion;
column15: To realize the TLF of associative memory, CA3-Pyr forms associations between different stimuli (object/space/context) presented in temporal proximity, and recalls the other stimulus when one is presented later. Input: object information from [U.LEC-L2] ([LEC-L2] object feature representation), spatial information from [U.MEC-L2] ([MEC-L2] spatial location and movement information), pattern-separated representation from [U.DG] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation), recurrent input from [U.CA3-Pyr] itself ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), and inhibitory signals from [U.CA3-IN] ([CA3-IN] engram-specific inhibitory signals). Output: representation of associated stimulus pairs provided by [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs).
column16: Interface integrates information from multiple input sources (direct EC input, mossy fibers from DG, self-recurrent, inhibitory input) and outputs to CA3-Pyr itself, CA3-IN, and neurons in CA1 region. This realizes the function described in Requirement: association formation and recall of multiple stimuli. Particularly, the recurrent connection ([U.CA3-Pyr] → [U.CA3-Pyr]) is the foundation of pattern completion.
column17: Heteroassociative memory and pattern completion: Computational function to learn associations between different input patterns and recall complete patterns from partial cues. This function is based on theoretical models of CA3 proposed by Marr (1971) and McNaughton & Morris (1987). CA3 recurrent connections function as a Hopfield-type attractor network, storing memory patterns as attractor states (Rolls, 2013). Recent computational studies show that heterosynaptic plasticity stabilizes engram formation through selective inhibition (Sanchez-Aguilera et al., 2025). Diamantaki et al. (2024) showed that human CA3 has sparse, high-precision connections that maximize associational power.
column18: CA3-Pyr strengthens synaptic connections between co-activated neurons through Hebbian learning in recurrent connections (cells that fire together, wire together). Specifically: (1) During encoding, NMDA receptor-dependent LTP is induced between CA3-Pyr neuron populations activated by simultaneously presented stimuli A and B. (2) During recall, when a partial cue of stimulus A activates part of CA3-Pyr, neuron populations corresponding to stimulus B are also activated through recurrent connections (pattern completion). (3) Selective inhibition from CA3-IN suppresses competing engrams, improving recall precision. (4) Strong input from mossy fibers promotes formation of novel patterns (detonator effect).
column19: [U.CA3-Pyr](t+1) = f(W_rec * [U.CA3-Pyr](t) + W_DG * [U.DG](t) + W_EC * ([U.LEC-L2](t) + [U.MEC-L2](t)) - [U.CA3-IN](t)), where W_rec is the recurrent weight matrix (Hebbian: ΔW_rec ∝ [U.CA3-Pyr]_pre * [U.CA3-Pyr]_post), f is a nonlinear activation function

Comment: Within ROI. CA3 inhibitory interneurons. Suppress competing engrams through selective inhibition to improve pattern completion precision and stability.
Requirement: [CA3-IN] Engram-specific inhibitory signals. Suppression of competing memory patterns;
Requirement realization by interface: During associative memory recall, when multiple memory engrams are partially activated, only the correct memory must be selectively recalled and competing memories suppressed. Input: feedforward input from [U.DG] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation) and excitatory input from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs). Output: engram-specific inhibitory signals from [U.CA3-IN] ([CA3-IN] engram-specific inhibitory signals) that selectively suppress competing engrams in [U.CA3-Pyr].
Capability: Interface receives excitatory input from [U.DG] and [U.CA3-Pyr] and sends inhibitory output to [U.CA3-Pyr]. This matches the function defined in Requirement: selective suppression of competing engrams.
Mechanism: Selective inhibition through heterosynaptic plasticity: Computational function to learn engram-specific inhibitory patterns and suppress competing engrams during memory recall. The model by Sanchez-Aguilera et al. (2025) showed that heterosynaptic plasticity at E-to-I synapses associates interneurons with specific engrams and selectively suppresses other engrams during recall. This function substantially enhances recall stability and precision compared to traditional global inhibition.
Implementation: CA3-IN is co-activated with specific engrams (CA3-Pyr activity patterns) during encoding, and heterosynaptic plasticity is induced at E-to-I synapses. During recall, when that engram is activated by a partial cue, associated CA3-INs are also activated and selectively suppress CA3-Pyr neurons of competing engrams. This selective inhibition stabilizes convergence to the correct engram attractor state. Feedforward inhibition from DG also prevents interference between novel and existing patterns via CA3-IN.
column12: [U.CA3-IN](t) = g(W_DG_IN * [U.DG](t) + W_CA3_IN * [U.CA3-Pyr](t)), where W_CA3_IN is subject to heterosynaptic plasticity: ΔW_CA3_IN ∝ [U.CA3-Pyr]_pre * (learning_signal), g is a nonlinear activation. Inhibition to CA3-Pyr: I_inh = W_IN_CA3 * [U.CA3-IN](t), where W_IN_CA3 is engram-specific

Comment: Within ROI. CA1 pyramidal cells. Stabilize associative memories received from CA3 and provide feedback to EC. Involved in spatial learning and memory retrieval.
Implementation: [CA1-Pyr] Stabilized associative memory representation. Spatiotemporal integration and memory retrieval output;
column12: For the TLF of associative memory, CA1-Pyr stabilizes associative memories formed in CA3 and transforms them into a form that can be stored as long-term memory. Input: Schaffer collateral input from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), temporoammonic input from [U.MEC-L3] and [U.LEC-L3] ([MEC-L3] spatial information and temporal control signals, [LEC-L3] contextual information), inhibitory input from [U.CA1-PV] and [U.CA1-SST] ([CA1-PV] perisomatic inhibitory signals, [CA1-SST] distal dendritic inhibitory signals). Output: stabilized associative memory representation from [U.CA1-Pyr] ([CA1-Pyr] stabilized associative memory representation) fed back to [U.EC-L5] and [U.EC-L2/3].
column13: Interface integrates main input from CA3 and direct input from EC, generates output to EC under precise control by inhibitory interneurons. This matches the function defined in Requirement: stabilization and output of associative memory. Integration of both CA3 and EC Layer 3 inputs is the foundation of heterosynaptic plasticity (Pena et al., 2026).
column14: Memory stabilization and consolidation: Computational function to transform temporary associative memories formed in hippocampal CA3 into long-term stable representations and provide feedback to cortex. This function is based on systems consolidation theory (Squire & Alvarez, 1995) and CA1 information integration model (Hasselmo, 2005). Wang et al. (2025) showed that progressive stabilization of CA1 place cells contributes to memory formation. CA1 replays memories during sharp wave-ripple (SWR) events from CA3 and propagates them to cortex, promoting memory consolidation (Buzsaki, 2015).
column15: CA1-Pyr integrates inputs from two pathways: CA3 and EC Layer 3. (1) Early in learning, CA3 input dominates and associative patterns formed in CA3 are transmitted to CA1. (2) BTSP (Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity) is induced within CA1, stabilizing place cells (Wang et al., 2025). (3) Plastic inhibition (iLTD/iLTP) by CA1-PV and CA1-SST adjusts the balance between CA3 and EC inputs, promoting memory consolidation (Udakis et al., 2020). (4) Stabilized memories are transmitted to cortex through feedback pathways from CA1 to EC. (5) Hierarchical temporal structure of theta and gamma oscillations controls timing of encoding and retrieval.
column16: [U.CA1-Pyr](t) = h(W_CA3 * [U.CA3-Pyr](t) + W_EC * ([U.MEC-L3](t) + [U.LEC-L3](t)) - W_PV * [U.CA1-PV](t) - W_SST * [U.CA1-SST](t)), where W_CA3 and W_EC are subject to heterosynaptic LTP, h is a nonlinear activation. Stabilization: ΔW_CA3 ∝ BTSP([U.CA1-Pyr], place_field)

Comment: Within ROI. CA1 parvalbumin-positive interneurons. Target perisomatic regions to control spike timing and network oscillations. Exhibit iLTD.
Output Semantics: [CA1-PV] Perisomatic inhibitory signals. Control of spike timing and theta oscillations;
Requirement: For associative memory stabilization, spike timing of CA1-Pyr and network oscillations (theta) must be precisely controlled to enable appropriate encoding and retrieval of information. Input: Schaffer collateral input from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs). Output: perisomatic inhibitory signals from [U.CA1-PV] ([CA1-PV] perisomatic inhibitory signals) that control spike timing of [U.CA1-Pyr].
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives feedforward excitation from [U.CA3-Pyr] and sends inhibitory output to soma vicinity of [U.CA1-Pyr]. This matches the function defined in Requirement: control of spike timing and oscillations.
Capability: Feedforward inhibition and spike timing control: Computational function to restrict firing time window of pyramidal cells through feedforward inhibition and achieve precise spike timing within theta oscillation phase. PV interneurons can fire at high frequency and function as pacemakers of theta oscillations (Buzsaki & Wang, 2012). Udakis et al. (2020) showed that PV-iLTD is activity-dependently induced and dynamically adjusts balance of inputs from CA3 and EC.
Mechanism: CA1-PV rapidly activates upon receiving excitatory input from CA3 and provides strong inhibition to soma and axon initial segment of CA1-Pyr. (1) Feedforward inhibition narrows firing time window of CA1-Pyr, promoting coincidence detection. (2) Rhythmic firing of PV interneurons generates and maintains theta oscillations. (3) iLTD via T-type calcium channels plastically changes PV→CA1-Pyr connections according to activity patterns, supporting place cell stabilization and environmental representation switching (Udakis et al., 2020).
Implementation: [U.CA1-PV](t) = k(W_CA3_PV * [U.CA3-Pyr](t)), inhibition: I_PV(t) = W_PV_CA1 * [U.CA1-PV](t), where W_PV_CA1 undergoes iLTD: ΔW_PV_CA1 < 0 upon high activity (T-type Ca2+ channel dependent), k is a fast-spiking nonlinear activation

Comment: Within ROI. CA1 somatostatin-positive interneurons. Target distal dendrites to control synaptic plasticity and calcium signaling. Exhibit iLTP.
Output Semantics: [CA1-SST] Distal dendritic inhibitory signals. Modulation of synaptic plasticity and calcium signaling;
Requirement: For associative memory stabilization, synaptic plasticity and calcium signaling occurring in distal dendrites of CA1-Pyr must be controlled to modulate input integration from CA3 and EC. Input: Schaffer collateral input from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs). Output: distal dendritic inhibitory signals from [U.CA1-SST] ([CA1-SST] distal dendritic inhibitory signals) that control distal dendrites of [U.CA1-Pyr].
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives feedforward excitation from [U.CA3-Pyr] and sends inhibitory output to distal dendrites of [U.CA1-Pyr]. This matches the function defined in Requirement: modulation of synaptic plasticity and calcium signaling.
Capability: Dendritic inhibition and input-specific plasticity control: Computational function to modulate integration of temporoammonic input from EC and Schaffer collateral input from CA3 through inhibition to distal dendrites, and control location-dependent synaptic plasticity. SST interneurons modulate local calcium signals and synaptic plasticity in dendrites (Lovett-Barron et al., 2012). Udakis et al. (2020) showed that SST-iLTP is activity-dependently induced and reprioritizes balance of CA3 and EC inputs.
Mechanism: CA1-SST activates upon receiving excitatory input from CA3 and provides inhibition to distal dendrites of CA1-Pyr. (1) Distal dendritic inhibition modulates influence of temporoammonic input from EC. (2) iLTP via T-type calcium channels strengthens SST→CA1-Pyr connections according to activity patterns, changing sensitivity to EC input (Udakis et al., 2020). (3) This plasticity causes CA1 to shift from CA3-dependent to EC-dependent as learning progresses. (4) SST interneuron inhibition controls dendritic spikes and calcium signals, promoting location-specific synaptic plasticity.
Implementation: [U.CA1-SST](t) = m(W_CA3_SST * [U.CA3-Pyr](t)), inhibition: I_SST(t) = W_SST_CA1_distal * [U.CA1-SST](t), where W_SST_CA1_distal undergoes iLTP: ΔW_SST_CA1_distal > 0 upon activity (T-type Ca2+ channel dependent), m is a regular-spiking nonlinear activation

Comment: noROI(output). Receives disynaptic feedback from CA1 and mediates object memory encoding (homosynaptic potentiation).
noROI(output). Receives monosynaptic feedback from CA1 and supports memory recall (heterosynaptic plasticity). Generates feedforward inhibition from CA1 input.
